7	I was born in nineteen twelve at the top end of Ostrey Hollow, in the house my father's father put up, and except for two years down at Ashlin when I was first married I have never lived anywhere else, and I would not count those two years anyhow. My father hauled milk to the station the same as everybody up here did. There were nine families of us hauling to that station and we were in and out of each other's kitchens the whole year round and I could name you every one of them, but you don't want names, you want the trouble, they always want the trouble.

9	The station stood at the very top of the Hollow where the road bends and then goes to nothing but the ridge. It was a low building, whitewashed, cold as a spring house inside even in August, and it smelled of milk and steam and hot iron, and you could hear the engine going before you came round the last turn. Ansel Keddie ran it. He went up there in ninety-five, the year before they opened it, to get it ready, and he tested that first summer too, and he was still there when I was a girl big enough to ride on the wagon with my father, so you can count that up and see how long a man can stand in one room.

11	He kept a book. I want to say about that book because everybody knew about it, it wasn't any secret thing. It was ruled, and the ruling was his own, done with a straightedge, and every line in it was the same height as every other line, and his figures were like print. He wrote in it standing up at a slope desk by the window where the light came in. If a man came in and asked him what his milk had done, he did not have to hunt. He turned to the day and he read it off. He tested a thousand cans a week and never a blot in that book, and I heard my father say more than once that if the rest of the world kept its accounts the way Ansel Keddie kept his there would be no lawyers in Ashlin. Which was my father's way of talking. There are still lawyers in Ashlin.

13	Now. Nineteen nineteen. That is the year everything went sour up here and I was seven years old and I remember it the way you remember a smell. A letter came from the Association, printed, over the manager's signature, and it said there was water in the cans coming down from Ostrey Hollow. That is what it said. Water in the cans. It went to nine families and my father was one of the nine and he read it at the table with his hat still on, which he never did, and my mother stood at the stove with her back to him and did not turn around the whole time he read it. He read it twice. Then he put it in the drawer of the desk in the front room and it was still in that drawer when he died and I believe my brother has it yet. Some of them kept theirs till they died. One woman I knew had hers pinned inside the lid of her trunk. You can tell people a thing like that is only business and they will still keep the paper forty years to prove what was said of them.

The curd comes soft and it will not knit; you get a slack, weak body and your yield is down, and you can stand at the vat and see your money going out with the whey. It cannot be hidden from the man who makes the cheese, because the cheese tells him, and it tells him the next morning, not next year. Butter is more forgiving that way. Cheese is a witness. ## Story 1 — The Association and the rule that made a station's word final (1889–1893)

**Who:** Gideon Vose and the farmers of the Larrow Valley.

**What happened:** In 1889 valley farmers, tired of hauling butter to Ashlin merchants and taking whatever price was allowed them, met at the Larrow Green schoolhouse and organized the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association. Gideon Vose was elected first president (he held the office 1889–1911, twenty-two years) and personally drafted the by-laws. The main creamery was built at Larrow Green, on Larrow Creek, in 1891, and the valley began to be paid in cash monthly for the first time. The critical rule, Article VII, provided that a patron is paid according to the butterfat his milk is found by test to contain, not its weight — and that "the test of the station where he delivers shall govern," with no appeal to any other test.

**When:** Founding 1889; creamery built 1891. The exact year Article VII itself was adopted is disputed: Effie Loomis, the Association's own secretary, dates it to 1892 (annual meeting following the creamery's opening); Dell Rundle's 1939 jubilee pamphlet dates it to 1891 (the year the churn was set up); Nyle Grigg's 1919 letter says 1893, hedged as "as I have always understood it." ## Story 5 — The state inspector condemns the glass (1907–1923)

**Who:** Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector for the Ordell circuit.

**What happened:** Strawn rode the circuit from 1907 to 1936, visiting Ostrey Hollow roughly once a year: checking scales against sealed weights, testing for added water with a lactometer, and watching the tester make a test start to finish. From 1908 on, every single recorded visit found no added water at that station — directly contradicting the manager's later water theory. Strawn had no way to check the station's pipettes against an outside standard until the state began issuing calibrated burettes to field inspectors in 1921; he carried his own for two seasons before finally using it there. On 12 June 1923 he ran the station's milk pipettes against the burette, found "these measures will not deliver their mark," condemned the entire crate on the spot, and told the manager to order new glass. New pipettes were in use by July 1923, and Strawn confirmed on his October 1923 visit that they now delivered their mark. He recorded the finding as routine equipment failure and drew no inference whatsoever about the station's preceding 26 years of figures. The Association wrote to Ammon & Sons on 28 June 1923 for replacements; the firm answered 2 July that its 1890s records could say nothing about the original lot. From 1924 the station's own test book and Strawn's own contemporaneous entry both record the average settling at 3.80 (elsewhere misremembered as 3.85 or 3.90).

**When:** condemnation 12 June 1923; new glass in service by July 1923; recovery visible from 1924.

**Quantities:** burette program from 1921; average rose from 3.61 to 3.80 the year after new glass arrived.

**Documents:** Strawn's own 1936 circuit-book extracts (his 1907–1936 pocket notebooks)]

## Section C — Math

### C1.

**(a) Proportion of the shortfall, from the glassware.**
The pipettes were blown to deliver 17.6 c.c. Ivy Keddie's own signed measurement sheet (9 March 1958), reproduced verbatim in her own talk and in curator Halbert Nym's catalogue (Item 14), gives the mean of five runs on each of nine pipettes as: 16.70, 16.71, 16.72, 16.72, 16.72, 16.73, 16.73, 16.74, 16.71. Sum = 150.48; ÷9 = **16.72 c.c.**
Ratio = 16.72 ÷ 17.6 = **0.95** exactly (check: 17.6 × 0.95 = 16.72). So the glass delivered 95% of its mark — a shortfall of **5%, "one part in twenty."**
I reject the figure of 16.27 c.c. that appears in Leland Vaught's own bulletin (Section III) and in the Ashlin Chronicle: it does not match the primary measurement sheet (which two separate documents quote identically as 16.72), it produces a ratio (0.9244) inconsistent with the "one part in twenty" language the *same* bulletin uses in its own conclusion, and 16.72/17.6 resolves to the suspiciously clean 0.95 while 16.27/17.6 does not resolve to anything the sources otherwise use. I treat 16.27 as a digit transposition of 16.72 (see Section E).

**(b) True average test, and the shortfall in points.**
Recorded average from 1898 on: **3.61** (the test book's own summary leaf, confirmed by Loomis's ledger reference and Falke's report).
True average = 3.61 ÷ 0.95 = **3.80** exactly (check: 3.80 × 0.95 = 3.61).
Shortfall = 3.80 − 3.61 = **0.19 point** ("nineteen hundredths"), matching Ivy Keddie's own stated gap and Hazel Brant's independent recollection.
